policy_title: Introduce a wealth tax and reform capital gains and inheritance taxes
stated: Introduce an annual wealth tax of 1% on assets above £10 million and 2% on assets above £1bn. Align Capital Gains Tax rates with income tax and NIC rates on employment income, reform inheritance tax, and remove the Upper Earnings Limit on National Insurance.

source.quote: Elected Greens will push for a wealth tax. This will tax the wealth of individual taxpayers with assets above £10 million at 1% and assets above £1bn at 2% annually. Elected Greens will push too for the reform Capital Gains Tax (CGT) by aligning the rates paid by taxpayers on income and taxable gains. Elected Greens will also call for the reform of tax rates on investment income, by aligning them with the tax and NIC rates on employment income. We would remove the Upper Earnings Limit that restricts the amount of National Insurance paid by high earners. We would reform inheritance tax, ensuring that intergenerational transfers of wealth are taxed more fairly.

bearing_set.reason: Removing the Upper Earnings Limit on NI directly cuts take-home pay for employees above ~£50,270; aligning CGT with income-tax-plus-NIC rates materially raises the effective tax on returns for business owners and investors who currently take income as capital gains — both are non-negligible effects on real wages and earnings fairness across income types.

Aligning CGT rates with income tax for property investors significantly changes the tax cost of holding and selling investment property, plausibly prompting sell-offs (affecting rental supply and owner-occupier supply) or deterring new buy-to-let investment — a contested but material lever on housing-market dynamics.
All four measures (wealth tax, CGT alignment, IHT reform, UEL removal) directly reduce after-tax income or after-tax wealth for affected individuals — a real O11 verdict on take-home money.

The package is explicitly revenue-raising; if behavioural responses are limited, it improves the funded/borrowed balance; if avoidance/flight is large, projected yield falls — a genuine contested fiscal verdict routed here.

CGT alignment with income-tax-plus-NIC rates and an annual wealth tax create concrete, IFS/OBR-modelled mechanisms — reduced post-tax return to investment, potential capital flight, lock-in effects, and disincentives to entrepreneurial exit — that would move business-investment and productivity indicators.

Wealth tax targets assets >£10m, CGT reform hits capital-owning households, IHT reform affects intergenerational wealth transfers, and UEL removal raises taxes on higher earners — all narrow the income/wealth gap by design, producing a clear inequality verdict.

membership_note: Four fundamentals earn real verdicts: O11 (who pays and how much), O12 (net fiscal effect), O13 (investment and business-dynamism spillovers), and O14 (distributional direction of the package). Effects on O2 or O4 are indirect and below the non-negligible bar; O15 cohesion effects are too diffuse to pin to a concrete indicator.
